comments.author: @kourostatis
comments.text: Only the first-born daughter, called kanakara, inherited her mother’s gold, house and lands. The rest of the daughters got absolutely nothing and had to endure becoming their eldest sister’s servants, unable to marry because they had no dowry. The first born daughter, from an early age was treated with exceptional care, always wearing the best and most richly decorated clothes, and a gold necklace , called kolaina, heavily decorated with many gold coins. The first born daughter also had the privilege to dance during the many festivals but her sisters had no such privilege. The kanakara usually married the first born son of a family, called kanakaris, who also inherited all his fathers lands and his brothers go nothing. The kanakaris had a special place to sit at church that nobody else could sit. They also dressed distinguishably from the other men. For instance they were the only ones that could wear a red fez. The claim that this was a matriarchal society is absurd. It was a highly class structured  society based on birth rights.

comments.author: @BeyondTheMapTV1
comments.text: Karpathos is fascinating because migration ended up reshaping family structure and property traditions in a very unusual way. 🇬🇷🏝 In villages like Olympos, women taking responsibility for land, homes and cultural continuity was not simply symbolic, it became part of how the community survived while men worked elsewhere. That connection between geography, migration and inheritance makes the island much more interesting than the title alone suggests.
